title: BeneBot at a Glance
description: Start with the operational README to understand BeneBot as a synthetic-data guide for one Jane Doe medical bill, not a general health-record assistant. It introduces the Spanish-first demo, the historical-versus-current evidence boundary, and the honest degraded modes that keep the experience useful when an external service is unavailable.

title: Enter the Demo
description: The root layout establishes a bilingual, Spanish-default application shell, while the landing page presents a clearly synthetic billing email and routes Jane Doe into the fixed invoice. Together they show how the demo begins with disclosure and a bounded scenario before any patient-specific server work occurs.
languageLesson: Next.js App Router layouts establish shared document metadata and presentation, while page modules define route-specific server-rendered entry points.

title: Read the Bill
description: The invoice page and bill components turn the opening scenario into a secure patient journey: first show the reconciled historical claim, then create a server-issued session before revealing the assistant. Source dates and labels are part of the product logic, preventing historical deductible amounts from being mistaken for today's remaining benefits.
languageLesson: The server page owns trusted data loading, while the client experience owns the interactive transition into a signed conversation; this split keeps secrets and patient scope out of the browser bundle.

title: Deterministic Money Boundary
description: BeneBot does not ask an LLM to calculate a bill. The billing types, EOB normalizer, and reconciliation functions produce a single deterministic structure, enforce the allowed-charge and responsibility equations within one cent, and suppress numerical narration when the source data does not reconcile.
languageLesson: Pure TypeScript functions and explicit result contracts make financial transformations independently testable. The LLM receives already-normalized values and wording constraints, not arithmetic authority.

title: Signed Trust Envelope
description: Building on the deterministic bill, BeneBot binds each short-lived JWT to one patient, invoice, EOB, coverage, encounter, provider, and payer. Shared contracts define the closed tool surface, while sanitized errors and server-only environment validation make every API route fail closed instead of trusting identifiers supplied later by the browser.
languageLesson: Zod-validated boundary objects and narrow TypeScript contracts turn untrusted request data into explicit, typed capabilities. A signed session is treated as a scope envelope, not merely a login flag.

title: Bilingual Concept Policy
description: The assistant's English and Spanish explanations come from a code-owned healthcare-billing dictionary and an adjudicated es-419 concept library, not improvised definitions. Prompt rules and per-tool prerequisites attach safe analogies, forbidden claims, fixed-language behavior, and server-confirmed evidence requirements to each concept before the voice model can narrate it.
languageLesson: Separating canonical domain language from model prompts makes bilingual behavior reviewable and versionable. The prompt orchestrates policy, while structured dictionaries remain the source of explanatory meaning.

title: Voice with Text Parity
description: The main conversation panel connects Deepgram's bilingual Agent experience to exactly five BeneBot tools and presents every call as running, confirmed, or failed. Deepgram uses a temporary server-issued token, matching Flux recognition and Aura voices for English or Spanish, while the deterministic text router preserves the same safe journey whenever voice is unavailable.
languageLesson: A React client may manage microphone state and render transcripts, but credentials and healthcare integrations stay behind authenticated routes. Tool schemas form a constrained bridge between probabilistic conversation and deterministic server actions.

title: Explain Historical Adjudication
description: The bill-context route is the historical evidence tool: it loads only the session-scoped EOB and invoice context, permits a visibly identified fixture fallback, and rejects unreconciled numbers. Its bilingual narration then states both the source and the temporal limitation, so the assistant never presents old adjudication as proof of current coverage.

title: Refresh Current Benefits
description: Current eligibility takes a separate route through the guarded Stedi test integration and receives its own check timestamp. The fixed Jane Doe request must match before any network call, ambiguous payer fields remain unknown, and a fallback is explicitly labeled as non-live rather than allowed to validate the historical claim.

title: Persist Confirmed Follow-Up
description: Medplum is both the source for scoped FHIR R4 billing context and the destination for confirmed workflow artifacts. The server adapter validates references before idempotently writing a billing-review Task or bounded Communication; the routes report success only after Medplum returns the persisted resource identifiers, and no full transcript is stored.
languageLesson: FHIR references are integrity constraints between resources, so dependent writes must validate the session-bound Patient, Encounter, EOB, and Coverage relationships before creating Task or Communication records.

title: Prove the Workflow
description: The staff page closes the loop by loading the server-confirmed eligibility, Task, and Communication artifacts into an accessible timeline beside the original EOB and invoice. This is the demo's operational proof: the patient-facing promise becomes a visible FHIR workflow, while seeded records remain clearly labeled when live Medplum is unavailable.

title: Safe Synthetic World
description: The fixed FHIR transaction bundle supplies the linked Jane Doe patient, payer, coverage, encounter, EOB, and invoice behind the whole tour, and the idempotent seed script can reproduce it in Medplum. Separate bilingual resource fixtures support hardship and billing-help searches without sending patient data to a search provider, while preserving fictional and community-reported disclosures.
languageLesson: Stable synthetic identifiers make repeated FHIR seeding idempotent and keep integration tests reproducible. Provenance fields travel with resource-search results so the UI cannot accidentally erase their disclosure status.

title: Evaluation Evidence Packet
description: BeneBot's conversation quality is grounded in an adjudicated packet rather than a vague notion of helpfulness. Canonical concepts, eight safety rubrics, 24 bilingual transcript cases, and an evidence-linked evaluation contract test historical/current separation, financial non-invention, tool ordering, confirmation, natural language, and safe analogies without promoting rejected material into runtime policy.

title: Verify Every Boundary
description: Focused unit and integration tests prove the architecture's hardest claims: exact one-cent bill reconciliation, safe bilingual prompting, tamper-resistant sessions, conservative Stedi normalization, and scoped Medplum writes. These tests turn the earlier design rules into executable gates and demonstrate that failed prerequisites prevent narration or persistence rather than producing plausible-looking success.

title: Rehearse the Whole Story
description: Finish with the browser test that rehearses the complete Spanish-first text path from synthetic email through bill explanation, current-benefit separation, interruption, confirmed follow-up, and staff-visible FHIR artifacts. The canonical build specification and package scripts show how that happy path is governed and how type-check, unit, build, and end-to-end checks turn the hackathon demo into a reproducible system.
languageLesson: Playwright tests behavior across real route and UI boundaries, while Vitest covers pure logic and server modules. Together they validate both the deterministic core and the user's end-to-end experience.
